text: The details of the NATALEE trial design and participants were described previously ( 22 , 37 ). Briefly, NATALEE—an international, randomized, open-label, phase III trial—enrolled patients with HR+/HER2− EBC who were randomized (1:1) to either receive ribociclib (400 mg/day, orally once daily, on a 3-week-on, 1-week-off schedule, for 36 months) plus an NSAI [either letrozole (2.5 mg/day) or anastrozole (1 mg/day), orally, for 60 months] or an NSAI alone ( 37 ). Premenopausal women and men in both arms were also administered goserelin (at a dose of 3.6 mg subcutaneously once every 4 weeks) for gonadal suppression. NSAI treatment could continue beyond the 60-month trial period per investigator’s clinical judgment, but it was not considered a trial treatment. Randomization was stratified based on menopausal status (men or premenopausal and postmenopausal women), anatomic stage II or III, receipt of prior (neo)adjuvant chemotherapy, and geographic region. The trial enrolled 5,101 patients.

Women and men ≥18 years of age at trial entry with histologically confirmed HR+/HER2− EBC were eligible for the study ( 37 ). Eligible patients were required to have anatomic stage II or III disease following the American Joint Committee on Cancer eighth edition anatomic staging. All patients with stage IIB and stage III disease were eligible, regardless of nodal involvement. Patients with stage IIA disease were eligible if they had at least one lymph node involved (N1), or if no lymph node was involved (N0), these patients were required to either have a grade 3 tumor or a grade 2 tumor with Ki-67 ≥20% or with high-genomic risk factors. High-genomic risk was classified based on an Oncotype DX recurrence score of ≥26 or categorization as high risk by Prosigna/PAM50, MammaPrint, or EndoPredict EPclin tests. Patients who had received any standard (neo)adjuvant ET for up to 12 months prior to randomization were eligible.

All participants provided written informed consent at enrollment. The study was approved by the participating site’s institutional review board or independent ethics committee and was performed in accordance with the Good Clinical Practice guidelines and the provisions of the Declaration of Helsinki. This trial is registered at ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT03701334 ).

section: Patients and Methods > HRQOL endpoints and assessments
text: This study utilized established patient-reported outcome (PRO) instruments to measure HRQOL from the patient’s perspective. The instruments used were as follows: the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC; RRID:SCR_004070) core quality of life questionnaire (EORTC QLQ-C30, version 3.0), the supplementary EORTC breast cancer–specific QOL questionnaire [EORTC QLQ-BR23 version 1.0 (for women)], the generic EuroQOL 5-level instrument (EQ-5D-5L), and the widely used Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) questionnaire ( 38 – 40 ).

section: Patients and Methods > HRQOL endpoints and assessments
text: The prespecified primary HRQOL endpoint of interest was the physical functioning (five items) domain score of the EORTC QLQ-C30. The prespecified secondary HRQOL endpoints included scores for the following domains: the global health status (GHS)/QOL (two items), the emotional functioning (four items), and the social functioning (two items) domains of the EORTC QLQ-C30; the breast symptoms (four items) of the EORTC QLQ-BR23; the visual analog scale (VAS) of EQ-5D-5L; and the anxiety and depression (seven items each) domain scores of the HADS questionnaire. Other domains of these PRO scores, not described here, were not part of the prespecified HRQOL analysis.

section: Patients and Methods > HRQOL endpoints and assessments
text: The scoring for these questionnaires followed the scoring procedures defined in each manual. The individual items of the EORTC were assessed using questions that can be answered on a raw scale of 1 (not at all) to 4 (very much), apart from the two items of the GHS domain that ranged from 1 (very poor) to 7 (excellent). As per the scoring manual, total scores for each domain scale were calculated and rescaled to a range of 0 to 100. A high score on functional domains represents a high level of functioning, whereas a high score on symptomatic domains represents more severe symptoms ( 41 ). The VAS of EQ-5D-5L, which ranges from 0 to 100, captures the patient’s rating of overall health status—higher scores represent better self-rated health states ( 39 ). Each individual item of HADS is scored on a scale of 0 (no impairment) to 3 (severe impairment).

The PRO assessments were conducted at the beginning of the patient’s visit prior to any clinical assessments, drug dosing, or diagnostic testing so as not to bias the patient’s perspective. Patients completed these questionnaires initially at screening and, then during treatment, every 12 weeks (±2 weeks) during the first 24 months and every 24 weeks (±3 weeks) thereafter until distant recurrence occurred or at the end of treatment (EOT; defined as discontinuation of all treatment components). PROs were also assessed at the confirmation of first recurrence and at the confirmation of distant recurrence (if the first recurrence was not a distant recurrence). After confirmation of distant recurrence, patients were assessed every 12 weeks for 12 months (±2 weeks; if confirmation of distant recurrence happened during the first 24 months from randomization) or every 24 weeks for 12 months (±3 weeks; if confirmation of distant recurrence happened after the first 24 months from randomization; Supplementary Table S1). No additional QOL follow-up assessments were conducted. Collection of all PRO measures had a ±3-day window unless otherwise indicated. PROs were collected from patients using paper forms in their local language.

All HRQOL analyses were performed in the intent-to-treat population and only included QOL data from patients prior to any recurrence. HRQOL data were categorized as fully completed, partially completed (defined as ≥1 item completed but not all items completed), or not completed based on the extent of completion of the questionnaires. Descriptive statistics (mean ± SE) were used to summarize the descriptive HRQOL scores at each scheduled assessment. EOT values were not included when summarizing the descriptive mean scores for the treatment period.

A compound symmetry time-categorical repeated-measures model was used to compare the changes in adjusted HRQOL scores from baseline within both treatment arms, as well as the between-treatment arms differences at scheduled time points during treatment. The time-categorical model allowed increased flexibility, with the aim of a better data fit for domains that did not follow a linear trend.

For the EORTC QLQ-C30, the longitudinal changes in the model-adjusted mean scores from baseline in both treatment arms were qualitatively compared with previously reported thresholds for interpretation of meaningful changes over time in mean subdomain scores ( 42 ). These published thresholds have been derived from combining a systematic review of published studies, expert opinions, and meta-analyses of relevant longitudinal studies reporting QLQ-C30 data ( 42 ). Small changes in the mean score—categorized as trivial in Cocks and colleagues ( 42 )—were not considered meaningful, and larger changes were classified as small, medium, or large meaningful deteriorations or improvements (Supplementary Table S2). Likewise, for the between-treatment arms difference in EORTC QLQ-C30 scores, adjusted mean scores at scheduled time points were qualitatively compared with previously published between-group thresholds for each domain (Supplementary Table S3; ref. 43 ).

Other QOL scores were compared against the commonly accepted ballpark of 0.5 × SD of their baseline values, including the QLQ-C30 emotional functioning domain score for which between-group thresholds have not been specified ( 43 , 44 ). This analysis included all assessments up to the time point at which there are ≥50 patients in each treatment arm (Supplementary Table S4).

A protocol-specified, time-continuous repeated-measures model (mixed-effects linear model with exchangeable covariance) was also used to compare the model-adjusted estimated mean changes in HRQOL scores from baseline over time in the two treatment arms, taking into account the baseline scores, stratification factors (anatomic stage, geographic location, prior chemotherapy, and menopausal status), time, and treatment–time interaction. Time was considered a linear continuous covariate expressed in months. Only patients with an evaluable baseline score and at least one evaluable postbaseline score were included in this analysis. All data collected, including EOT, were used to fit the model. Statistical Analysis System 9.4 (RRID:SCR_008567) was used for statistical modeling.

At the data cutoff of January 11, 2023 [median duration of follow-up (randomization to data cutoff), 34.0 months], 1,984 of 2,549 patients (78%) were receiving either ribociclib plus NSAI or NSAI alone in the ribociclib plus NSAI arm, whereas 1,826 of 2,552 patients (72%) were on treatment in the NSAI alone arm (Supplementary Fig. S2; ref. 22 ). A total of 515 of the 2,549 patients (20%) completed 3 years of ribociclib treatment in the ribociclib plus NSAI arm, and 862 (33.8%) had stopped ribociclib early but were still receiving NSAI ( 22 ).

At baseline, the majority of patients who were assessed with PRO questionnaires in the ribociclib arm ( n = 2,495; 97.9%) and NSAI alone arm ( n = 2,483; 97.3%) had partially or fully completed them. At week 13 (first PRO assessment time point after baseline), 2,353 patients in the ribociclib arm and 2,218 patients in the NSAI alone arm were included in the assessment, of which 2,279 (96.8%) and 2,149 (96.9%) had partially or fully completed them, respectively. At week 169, the last on-treatment PRO assessment that was included in the analysis per statistical analysis plan (≥50 patients in each arm), a relatively lower number of patients (262 in the ribociclib arm and 265 in the NSAI alone arm) had HRQOL assessments, of which 245 (93.5%) and 246 (92.8%) had partially or fully completed them, respectively. At EOT (due to any reason including early discontinuations), 469 of 544 (86.2%, ribociclib arm) and 502 of 610 (82.3%, NSAI alone arm) patients who were analyzed for HRQOL had partially or fully completed them (Supplementary Table S4). The mean scores at baseline for all HRQOL outcomes that were assessed in the study were similar between the ribociclib and the NSAI alone arm (Supplementary Table S5).

section: Results > Treatment effect on EORTC QLQ-C30 functional domain scores
text: For the physical functioning domain, the primary HRQOL endpoint of interest, deterioration in mean scores (using descriptive statistics) at first assessment (week 13) was similarly minimal in both the ribociclib (−1.21 points) and the NSAI alone (−1.22 points; Fig. 1A ) arms. The scores then remained stable with respect to baseline during treatment for both the ribociclib (1 year, −1.12 points; 3 years, −1.50 points) and the NSAI alone (1 year, −1.35 points; 3 years, −1.34 points) arms. Overall, no difference from baseline was observed in the time-categorical, model-adjusted mean score in either arm during treatment, based on published thresholds for interpreting longitudinal changes in the physical functioning score (−5 to 2, no difference; Fig. 1C ; Supplementary Table S2; ref. 42 ). Adjusted analyses also showed that the decrease in physical functioning score from baseline did not differ meaningfully between the two arms at any time point, based on the published between-group threshold of five points for physical functioning (Supplementary Table S3; ref. 43 ). Finally, an analysis with a linear-time, repeated-measures model also showed a similar decrease from baseline between the two treatment arms over time (Supplementary Fig. S1; Supplementary Table S6).

section: Results > Treatment effect on EORTC QLQ-C30 functional domain scores
text: For the GHS domain, the mean deterioration in scores from baseline at the first assessment in both treatment arms (ribociclib arm, −2.09 points; NSAI alone arm, −1.33 points; Fig. 1B ) was comparable. Following this, the scores stabilized in both arms with respect to baseline during treatment, with scores in the ribociclib arm (1 year, −2.77 points; 3 years, −3.10 points) being approximately 1 point lower, on average, than in the NSAI alone arm (1 year, −1.61 points; 3 years, −1.96 points). Overall, no difference from baseline was observed in the adjusted mean GHS score in either arm during treatment, based on published thresholds for interpreting GHS longitudinal changes (−5 to 5, no difference; Fig. 1D ; Supplementary Table S2; ref. 42 ). Furthermore, decreases in the adjusted GHS score from baseline did not meaningfully differ between the two treatment arms at any time point, based on the published between-group global QOL threshold of four points (Supplementary Table S3; ref. 43 ). The linear-time repeated measures model also showed a similar decrease from baseline between the arms over time (Supplementary Fig. S2; Supplementary Table S6).

section: Results > Treatment effect on EORTC QLQ-C30 functional domain scores
text: For the social functioning domain, an improvement in mean scores from baseline was observed at the first assessment in both arms (ribociclib arm, 1.77 points; NSAI alone arm, 2.61 points; Fig. 2A ). Following the week 13 assessment, the scores stabilized in both treatment arms with respect to baseline, with an approximately 1- to 2-point lower score in the ribociclib arm (1 year, 0.65 points; 3 years, 0.26 points) versus the NSAI alone arm (1 year, 1.82 points; 3 years, 1.39 points). Overall, during treatment, no difference from baseline was observed in the adjusted mean social functioning score in either arm, based on published thresholds for change in social functioning score (−6 to 3, no difference; Fig. 2C ; Supplementary Table S2; ref. 42 ). No meaningful difference between the ribociclib and NSAI alone arms was observed at any time point, based on the published between-group social functioning threshold of five points (Supplementary Table S3; ref. 43 ). The linear-time repeated measures model confirmed similar changes from baseline over time between the two arms (Supplementary Fig. S3; Supplementary Table S6).

section: Results > Treatment effect on EORTC QLQ-C30 functional domain scores
text: A deterioration in mean emotional functioning scores from baseline was observed in both the ribociclib arm (1 year, −3.15 points; 3 years, −4.52 points) and the NSAI alone arm (1 year, −4.45 points; 3 years, −3.97 points; Fig. 2B ). Overall, during treatment, no difference from baseline was observed in the adjusted mean emotional functioning score in either arm, based on previously published thresholds for longitudinal changes (emotional functioning: −3 to 6, no difference; Fig. 2D ; Supplementary Table S2; ref. 42 ). Furthermore, the decrease in adjusted emotional functioning score from baseline did not differ meaningfully between the two arms at any time point, with the scores in both treatment arms being within 0.5 SD of their baseline values, with the linear-time repeated-measures model confirming a similar decrease from baseline between the two arms over time (Supplementary Fig. S4; Supplementary Table S6).

section: Results > Treatment effect on EORTC QLQ-BR23 scores
text: An initial improvement in mean breast cancer symptom scores was observed in both treatment arms (ribociclib arm: −2.82 points; NSAI alone arm: −1.96 points) at week 13 ( Fig. 3A ). The improvement in this score continued as treatment continued, in the ribociclib (1 year, −4.53 points; 3 years, −6.04 points) and the NSAI alone (1 year, −4.64 points; 3 years, −7.89 points) arms. Overall, no difference from baseline was observed in adjusted mean breast cancer scores in either arm during treatment, with the scores being within 0.5 SD of their baseline values ( Fig. 3B ). Adjusted analyses showed that the decrease in breast cancer symptoms score from baseline did not differ meaningfully between the arms at any time point, with the scores being within 0.5 SD of their baseline values. Finally, analysis with a linear-time repeated-measures model showed a similar decrease from baseline between the two treatment arms over time (Supplementary Fig. S5; Supplementary Table S6).

section: Results > Treatment effect on EQ-5D-5L VAS scores
text: A minimal deterioration in mean VAS scores from baseline was initially observed at week 13 in both treatment arms (ribociclib arm, −1.32 points; NSAI alone arm, −0.79 points; Fig. 4A ). The scores stabilized later, with an approximately 1-point lower score in the ribociclib arm (1 year, −0.82 points; 3 years, −1.50 points) compared with the NSAI alone arm (1 year, −0.18 points; 3 years, 0.09 points) during treatment. Adjusted mean VAS scores in both treatment arms were within 0.5 SD of their baseline values during treatment, showing no difference from baseline ( Fig. 4B ). Likewise, decreases in adjusted VAS scores from baseline did not differ meaningfully between the two arms at any time point, as they were within 0.5 SD of their baseline values, and the linear-time repeated-measures model confirmed a similar decrease from baseline between the treatment arms over time (Supplementary Fig. S6; Supplementary Table S6).

section: Results > Treatment effect on HADS scores
text: The HADS anxiety and depression mean scores did not meaningfully increase from baseline during treatment in either arm ( Fig. 5A and B ). Overall, no difference from baseline was observed in adjusted mean HADS scores in either arm during treatment, with the scores being within 0.5 SD of their baseline values ( Fig. 5C and D ). Adjusted analyses showed that the increase in HADS scores from baseline did not differ meaningfully between the arms at any time point, with both the anxiety and depression scores in the ribociclib and NSAI alone arms being within 0.5 SD of their baseline values. Analysis using the linear-time repeated-measures model also showed a similar increase from baseline in HADS scores between the two treatment arms over time (Supplementary Fig. S7; Supplementary Table S6).

section: Results > Treatment effect on HADS scores
text: Finally, the representativeness of study participants is shown in Supplementary Table S7.

This study had some limitations. It was not powered to detect differences in QOL variables between the two treatment arms although the overall large sample size does help to provide reasonably precise estimates of the QOL differences as reflected in the results. Additionally, a low number of patients were assessed for HRQOL at week 169, the last assessment time point included in this analysis, due to patients discontinuing treatment early or being on study treatment and not yet reaching week 169 ( 22 ). Although the minimally important differences in QOL scores are well defined in the ABC setting, these thresholds are not defined in the EBC setting, making it challenging to interpret within-patient and between-treatments QOL score differences. Although not specific to EBC, previously published thresholds were used to guide the interpretation of meaningful changes in the current QOL data ( 42 – 44 ).
